bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Department of Labor to study building code requirements for single-staircase buildings up to six stories in Maryland and across North America, consulting with fire service representatives, a fire engineer, and an affordable housing advocate. The department must report findings and recommendations by December 1, 2026, on potential legislative or regulatory changes to authorize single-staircase construction to increase affordable multifamily housing.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Multifamily housing developers, affordable housing advocates and prospective tenants, firefighters, and local building code officials
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $58,222 in FY 2026 and $21,317 in FY 2027 to hire two temporary, part-time contractual staff (an assistant attorney general and a regulatory economist) to conduct the study and prepare the report. There is no effect on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MD Labor is the primary implementing agency tasked with conducting the study on building code requirements for single-staircase buildings, consulting with specified stakeholders, and submitting legislative and regulatory recommendations by December 1, 2026.
The Office of the State Fire Marshal is a division within the Maryland Department of State Police and is explicitly mandated by the bill to be consulted by MD Labor during the study.

The bill mandates consultation with a fire engineer who is a faculty member at a public institution of higher education with a fire protection program (specifically the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland, College Park).
The Department of Labor is required to report its findings and recommendations regarding building code modifications directly to the Governor by December 1, 2026.

bill_summary: Increases the threshold from $15,000 to $50,000 for contracts for services or supplies that require a competitive bidding process and associated requirements in St. Mary's County.
responsible_party: St. Mary's County Commissioners
stakeholders: St. Mary's County government, procurement officials, and vendors or contractors bidding on county contracts for services and supplies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. For local finances, the bill may generate operational efficiencies for St. Mary's County but does not materially affect county revenues or expenditures.

Synopsis: Authorizing the St. Mary's County Metropolitan Commission to discontinue all or part of water or sewer service provided to an improved private property determined to be unsafe, unfit, or unsuitable for human occupancy due to an accident, artificial disaster, or natural disaster; requiring the suspension of the ready-to-serve charge on certain private properties; and authorizing the St. Mary's County Metropolitan Commission to utilize certain remedies for a violation related to certain public water and sewer use.
Title: St. Mary's County - Metropolitan Commission - Discontinuance of Service

bill_summary: Authorizes the St. Mary’s County Metropolitan Commission (MetCom) to discontinue water or sewer service to private property deemed unsafe, unfit, or unsuitable for human occupancy due to an accident or disaster, and requires the suspension of ready-to-serve charges during that period. The bill also expands enforcement remedies for violations of public water and sewer rules and repeals the $1,000 cap on assessments for the reimbursement of actual costs incurred by MetCom.
responsible_party: St. Mary's County Metropolitan Commission
stakeholders: St. Mary's County property owners with damaged or uninhabitable properties, public water and sewer customers, and violators of MetCom water and sewer regulations.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not materially affected. MetCom expenditures are not materially affected, but local revenues may increase because the bill lifts the $1,000 cap on administrative cost reimbursement assessments, enabling MetCom to recover full actual costs for rule violations (for context, St. Mary's County reported $105,000 in uncollected costs across 11 violation incidents in FY 2025). MetCom may also experience a minor reduction in ready-to-serve fee revenue while service is suspended to uninhabitable properties.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission oversees public utility regulation across Maryland and served as an information source for the bill; however, the legislation directly amends St. Mary's County local laws governing the St. Mary's County Metropolitan Commission and has no material fiscal or operational impact on the State.

bill_summary: Authorizes the Director of Human Resources of Frederick County to request State and national criminal history records checks through the Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository for prospective and current county employees and volunteers, establishes confidentiality rules, and allows individuals to contest record findings.
responsible_party: Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository of the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Frederick County Director of Human Resources
stakeholders: Prospective and current employees and volunteers of Frederick County

bill_summary: The Recreational Equality for Service Members Act establishes uniform statutory definitions for military and uniformed service terms across Maryland law. It expands and codifies certain recreational benefits and privileges for active service members, Maryland National Guard members, and veterans, including free day-use and per-vehicle entry to State parks, as well as various hunting and fishing license exemptions and protections.
responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Active duty service members, members of reserve components and the Maryland National Guard, veterans (including commissioned officers of the Public Health Service and NOAA), and their families.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances because the expansion of privileges primarily applies to a relatively small population of commissioned officers in the Public Health Service and NOAA. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Natural Resources Article, requiring the Department of Natural Resources to administer updated rules, fee waivers, and license exemptions for active service members and veterans regarding State park admissions, recreational and commercial fishing licenses, and hunting licenses.

The bill updates the core statutory definitions in § 9-901 of the State Government Article governing the Department of Veterans and Military Families, including definitions for 'veteran', 'service member', 'active service member', 'military family', and 'uniformed services'.

The bill specifically amends Natural Resources § 1-405 governing the Chesapeake Bay Trust's administration of the Healing Hunting and Fishing Fund grants to include all service members rather than only armed forces members.

The bill explicitly establishes in Natural Resources § 5-1014 that any member of the Maryland National Guard is entitled to enter State parks without paying day-use entry fees or per-vehicle entry fees upon presenting a valid identification card.

Synopsis: Prohibiting transportation companies that transport children to residential child care programs from using certain restraints unless there is a substantial likelihood of imminent serious physical harm to a child or others; prohibiting transportation companies that transport children to residential child care programs from picking up children between the hours of 9 p.m. and 6 a.m.; authorizing an individual and the Attorney General to bring a certain civil action against certain transportation companies; and applying the Act prospectively.
Title: Residential Child Care Programs - Transportation Companies - Regulation (Preventing Abduction in Youth Transport Act of 2025)

bill_summary: Enacts the Preventing Abduction in Youth Transport Act of 2025, which regulates youth transportation companies transporting children to residential child care programs. It prohibits these companies from using visual impairments (such as blindfolds or hoods) and mechanical restraints, limits the use of physical restraints to situations with a substantial likelihood of imminent serious physical harm where no less restrictive alternative exists, and bars picking up children between 9:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. unless under contract with the Department of Human Services. It also authorizes the Attorney General and affected individuals to file civil actions for violations.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Children transported to residential child care programs, their families, youth transportation companies, and residential child care programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not substantively affect State or local governmental operations or finances. The Office of the Attorney General can implement the enforcement provisions using existing budgeted resources. There is potential for indeterminate statutory damages recovered through civil actions, but no specific revenue or expenditure figures are estimated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly empowers the Attorney General to initiate civil enforcement actions against youth transportation companies that violate restraint or transport time regulations, seeking injunctive relief and civil statutory damages.

The bill establishes an explicit exception to the restricted transport hours (9:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.) for youth transportation companies under contract with the Department of Human Services, and DHS licenses residential child care programs.
The Maryland Department of Health licenses residential child care and behavioral health programs whose incoming youth transported by private companies are subject to the bill's provisions.
The Department of Juvenile Services licenses residential child care programs and oversees justice-involved youth who may be subject to youth transport services governed under the bill.

The bill establishes a civil cause of action allowing individuals and the Attorney General to bring lawsuits against noncompliant transportation companies in state courts, with extended statutes of limitations.

bill_summary: The Procurement Reform Act of 2025 comprehensively alters Maryland State procurement law. It reorganizes procurement authority by expanding the responsibilities of the Chief Procurement Officer, creating an IT technical procurement team within the Department of Information Technology, and granting the Maryland Department of Transportation independent authority over transportation-related supplies and services. Additionally, it increases the Small Business Reserve contract threshold to $1 million, establishes requirements for contractors to use registered apprentices and interns on covered procurements, introduces a good labor practices evaluation factor, requires diversity plans for certain high-value contracts, accelerates State payment terms to 15 days for small businesses, and transfers programs and regulatory authorities to the Governor's Office of Small, Minority, and Women Business Affairs.
responsible_party: Department of General Services (Office of State Procurement / Chief Procurement Officer), Department of Information Technology, Maryland Department of Labor, and Governor's Office of Small, Minority, and Women Business Affairs
stakeholders: State contractors and vendors, small businesses, minority- and women-owned business enterprises (MBEs), veteran-owned small businesses (VSBEs), apprentices and student interns, and State procurement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $840,800 in FY 2026, which accounts for the October 1, 2025 effective date, rising to $1.16 million by FY 2030. This reflects the hiring of one assistant Attorney General for compliance and enforcement and six IT technical procurement staff members within the Department of Information Technology. State procurement costs across all funds may also increase due to reduced competition or vendor compliance costs. Special fund revenues from penalties are not anticipated to be material. Local government finances are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly reforms the State procurement code, expanding powers of the Chief Procurement Officer within DGS, altering DGS authority over IT and commodity procurement, adjusting small procurement oversight, and transferring the Employment Works Program out of DGS.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill assigns substantial new responsibilities to GOSBA, including receiving the Employment Works Program from DGS, promulgating regulations for workforce and supplier diversity plans, establishing criteria for the Veteran-Owned Small Business Reserve, and setting small business and MBE standards.

The bill mandates that DoIT establish a technical procurement team with technology and agile procurement expertise to assist state units, resulting in a direct general fund expenditure increase of $728,219 in FY 2026 for six new positions.

The bill charges the Department of Labor with administering and enforcing the new Internship and Registered Apprenticeship Program requirements on covered procurements, and tasks the Commissioner of Labor and Industry with administering the Good Labor Practices evaluation program.

The bill alters BPW oversight over source selection methods, requires updated regulations on expedited change orders, receives reports on expedited procurements and MBE waivers, and directs the BPW Procurement Advisor to conduct a study on in-state vendor preferences.

The bill grants MDOT independent procurement authority for transportation-related supplies and services, including IT services and supplies, streamlining transportation procurements, while maintaining MDOT representation on the Preferred Providers committee.

The bill grants MDTA, alongside MDOT, independent procurement authority over supplies and services (including IT supplies and services) for transportation-related activities without approval from other primary procurement units.

The bill requires OAG to determine whether to bring civil enforcement actions for violations of apprenticeship and internship requirements and consult on MBE/VSBE guidelines, resulting in an additional Assistant Attorney General position and $112,629 in FY 2026 expenditures.
The bill establishes a specialized Veteran-Owned Small Business Reserve program specifically applicable to all procurements conducted by or on behalf of DVMF.

The Adjutant General heads the Maryland Military Department, and the bill mandates that all procurements by the Military Department are subject to the newly established Veteran-Owned Small Business Reserve.
The bill explicitly requires the Department of Commerce to assist the Special Secretary for GOSBA in establishing procedures to compile small business bidder lists and locate potential MBE sources.
The bill requires MES to conduct triennial reviews and evaluations of all pay-for-success contracts completed by state agencies and be reimbursed by those agencies for its review costs.
The bill transfers authority from DBM to the Chief Procurement Officer regarding the approval of noncompetitive negotiation for classes of procurements.
DNR is specifically designated under § 13-228 as an authorized agency to enter into pay-for-success contracts for environmental outcomes projects.
MDE is specifically authorized under § 13-228 to enter into pay-for-success contracts for environmental outcomes.
MDA is explicitly authorized under § 13-228 to enter into pay-for-success contracts, including agricultural baseline water quality outcome contracts.
The bill amends mandatory statutory contract clauses governing the investigation of discrimination complaints involving contractors upon request of the Commission on Civil Rights.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Public Safety and Correctional Services serves on the statutory Pricing and Selection Committee for Preferred Providers, which is modified by the bill.
MSDE's Assistant Secretary for Vocational Rehabilitation serves on the statutory Pricing and Selection Committee for Preferred Providers, the membership of which is altered by the bill.

responsible_party: Maryland Department of Disabilities
stakeholders: Job seekers and employees with disabilities, as well as Maryland State government agencies and units
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no fiscal impact in FY 2026. Beginning in FY 2027, State general fund expenditures increase by at least $250,000 annually to modestly staff and operate ODEAP (covering two positions, contractual data services, assistive technology purchases, and operating expenses), with full implementation potentially requiring an additional $1.0 million annually. State revenues and local government operations and finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates the Office of Disability Employment Advancement and Policy (ODEAP) directly within the Department of Disabilities, charging the department with implementing and overseeing the Maryland as a Model Employer Initiative, administering associated funding, and submitting annual progress reports.

As the State's central personnel and budget agency, DBM oversees state employment rules, job classifications, and budget allocations, directly interfacing with the initiative's state government workforce recruitment, hiring, and retention policies.

This is an Administration initiative requiring annual reporting directly to the Governor on employment outcomes for people with disabilities in the state workforce, and authorizes discretionary executive budget appropriations starting in fiscal year 2027.

bill_summary: The Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act adjusts various aspects of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. Among other provisions, it reduces per-pupil target foundation amounts for fiscal years 2027 through 2035, alters and delays required expenditures for teacher collaborative time, and reduces mandated funding for the Coordinated Community Supports Partnership Fund. It also creates a mechanism to freeze major education funding increases if December state revenue estimates decline by 3.75% or more compared to March estimates. Additionally, the act establishes the Academic Excellence Program and Fund, the Maryland Teacher Relocation Incentive Grant, a national teacher recruitment campaign, modifies the Grow Your Own Educators Grant Program and school leadership training, and expands flexibility in expending Concentration of Poverty grants.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education
stakeholders: Maryland public school students, teachers, school administrators, local school systems, local boards of education, and local workforce development boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures decrease by $29.5 million in FY 2026 and by $156.1 million by FY 2030, driven largely by reductions in mandated Coordinated Community Supports Partnership funding and lower per-pupil foundation amounts. Special fund revenues increase by $602,700 in FY 2026 and $2.8 million in FY 2027 from interest earnings on higher Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund balances. Locally, LEAs receive an additional $19.4 million via the Grow Your Own Educators Program in FY 2026, but net local revenues and expenditures decrease significantly beginning in FY 2027 ($70.6 million reduction in FY 2027, growing to $194.4 million in FY 2030) due to decreased state aid and reduced required local appropriations. Delayed collaborative time mandates also provide LEAs with significant fiscal flexibility.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSDE is the primary implementing agency for the bill, responsible for administering major education aid formulas, the Academic Excellence Program and Fund, the Grow Your Own Educators Grant Program, teacher relocation incentives, community school implementation oversight, and school leadership training.

DBM oversees the state budget, which is directly impacted by altered mandated appropriations for public education, reductions to the Coordinated Community Supports Partnership Fund, statutory budget submission requirements for the Accountability and Implementation Board, and revenue-contingent funding limitations.

The State Treasurer is statutorily designated to hold and invest moneys in the newly created Academic Excellence Fund and ensure interest earnings are credited to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund.

The Comptroller is required to account for the newly established Academic Excellence Fund and manage the accounting of interest and revenues between special funds and the General Fund under State Finance and Procurement § 6-226.

The bill places direct statutory requirements on the Governor's budget submissions, including mandated appropriations for public schools and AIB without revision, specified CCSP funding, and mandatory limitations on budget growth during revenue shortfalls.

The bill temporarily pauses certain accessibility requirements for digital tools utilizing artificial intelligence under Education § 7-910, a section where the Secretary of Disabilities shares statutory oversight with the State Superintendent.

The bill extends local school funding distributions to local workforce development boards for the Career Counseling Program and incorporates registered teacher apprenticeships into teacher pipeline programs overseen in part by MD Labor.

The board and its CTE Committee have statutory roles in evaluating career counseling agreements and workforce readiness pathways, which are directly affected by the extension of the Career Counseling Program for Middle and High School Students.

The bill amends statutory per-pupil calculations and growth rate definitions that determine MSD's state funding formula to hold its funding levels constant amidst broader Blueprint formula alterations.

The bill explicitly allows county governing bodies to exceed local charter tax caps for the purpose of funding payments on behalf of local school boards to the Teachers' Pension System and Teachers' Retirement System administered by SRPS/SRA.
USM institutions are eligible partners and recipients of grant funding under the Grow Your Own Educators program, the Academic Excellence Fund, and research consultations for community schools.

bill_summary: The Chesapeake Bay Legacy Act establishes the Maryland Leaders in Environmentally Engaged Farming (LEEF) Program and its associated special fund to incentivize farmers to adopt conservation and community practices. The bill also incorporates regenerative practices and traditions into healthy soil definitions, establishes a statutory Water Quality Monitoring Program within the Department of Natural Resources (DNR), modifies fishery management plan requirements and coastal bay hearing rules, alters aquaculture leasing and protest processes, exempts licensed commercial finfish harvesters processing fish via ikejime from food establishment licensing, expedites permitting for Whole Watershed Restoration Partnership projects, and authorizes oyster restoration projects to generate water quality trading credits.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture, Department of Natural Resources, and Maryland Department of the Environment
stakeholders: Maryland agricultural producers and farmers, commercial and recreational fishers, charter boat captains, aquaculture leaseholders, restaurants, environmental and watershed restoration sponsors, and bay watershed communities.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $500,000 in FY 2026 (funded contingently in the state budget) and by a mandated $900,000 annually from FY 2027 through FY 2030 to support the LEEF Program Fund. Special fund revenues and expenditures reflect equivalent increases ($500,000 in FY 2026 and $900,000 annually from FY 2027 through FY 2030). DNR special fund revenues may increase by up to $13,725 annually from new aquaculture application and survey fees, as well as an indeterminate increase from water quality trading credits generated by state oyster restoration projects. Local government revenues may increase if local entities generate and sell water quality trading credits from locally funded oyster restoration projects.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 506 directly charges the Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA) with administering the newly established Leaders in Environmentally Engaged Farming (LEEF) Program and its special fund, setting conservation practice standards, and coordinating with other agencies, accompanied by a mandated annual appropriation.

The bill assigns major operational responsibilities to DNR, including establishing the statutory Water Quality Monitoring Program, revising fishery management plan requirements, reforming aquaculture leasing and fees, authorizing long-term agricultural leases for regenerative farming on DNR lands, and leading the Whole Watershed Restoration Partnership permitting process.

MDE is required to authorize oyster restoration projects to generate water quality trading credits and certify those credits by December 31, 2025. MDE also participates on the Whole Watershed Restoration Partnership State management team and has applicability rules clarified for stream and floodplain restoration permits.

The bill amends the Health - General Article to exempt commercial fishers who harvest and process finfish on a vessel using the ike jime method for direct sale to restaurants from MDH food establishment licensing requirements.

The bill statutorily tasks the Maryland Energy Administration with coordinating with the Maryland Department of Agriculture to establish incentives for farmers participating in the LEEF Program, particularly regarding on-farm renewable energy.

The Secretary of Planning designates a representative to serve on the Whole Watershed Restoration Partnership State management team, which is tasked with project selection and permitting coordination under the bill.
The bill impacts OAH case flow by permitting DNR to require mediation between protestants and aquaculture lease applicants prior to transmitting contested lease protests to OAH for adjudication.
The bill explicitly mandates that the Comptroller account for the newly created Maryland Leaders in Environmentally Engaged Farming (LEEF) Program Fund.
The bill statutorily requires the State Treasurer to hold the newly created Maryland Leaders in Environmentally Engaged Farming (LEEF) Program Fund separately as a special fund.

Synopsis: Clarifying a prohibition on including in State contracts provisions pertaining to limitations of liability for damage to real or tangible personal property; and clarifying a prohibition on including in State contracts provisions limiting the recovery of costs related to the use of replacement contractors under certain circumstances.
Title: State Contracts - Prohibited Provisions
bill_summary: Clarifies statutory prohibitions on certain terms in Maryland State contracts, specifically specifying that contracts cannot limit liability for damage to the State's real or tangible personal property and clarifying restrictions against limiting the State's ability to recover excess costs associated with using replacement contractors.
responsible_party: Maryland State procurement units and contracting agencies (including the Department of General Services, Department of Budget and Management, and the Board of Public Works)
stakeholders: State contractors, vendors doing business with Maryland, and State procurement officials
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State operations or finances, and local government finances and operations are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the State's central procurement authority responsible for public contracting, real estate, and facility management, DGS must ensure that all State procurement contracts comply with the updated prohibitions on liability limitation and replacement contractor cost provisions.

The OAG reviews State contracts for legal sufficiency and form, represents State agencies in contract drafting and disputes, and enforces statutory prohibitions against void contractual terms such as improper limitation of liability.
The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant State procurement contracts and expenditures, ensuring that contracts submitted for State approval conform to State procurement law.

MDOT enters into extensive procurement contracts across its modal administrations for transit, highways, and infrastructure, requiring compliance with the revised limits on replacement contractor costs and property damage liability.
DoIT executes major statewide technology procurement contracts where liability limitation clauses and replacement contractor terms are critical negotiation and compliance elements.
DBM regulates and manages statewide service contracts and state fiscal operations, requiring adherence to revised procurement standards across Executive Branch agencies.

The Treasurer's Office manages the State Insurance Trust Fund, which handles liability and property damage claims for the State, and holds a voting seat on the Board of Public Works overseeing procurement contracts.
AOC procures judicial branch goods and services and supports the court system, which interprets and enforces State contract dispute actions and determinations of void contract clauses.

bill_summary: This bill expands state procurement preferences for Blind Industries and Services of Maryland (BISM) by requiring prime contractors on State maintenance contracts with housekeeping or janitorial components to procure janitorial products that are packaged or repackaged by BISM, to the extent practicable and when available.
responsible_party: State procurement units and State or State-aided or controlled entities
stakeholders: Blind Industries and Services of Maryland (BISM), prime contractors on State maintenance contracts, and small businesses that supply janitorial products
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to have a direct effect on State finances, though it may have a minimal operational effect on State procurement units. It is not expected to materially affect local government finances or operations. Small businesses providing janitorial supplies may experience fewer subcontracting or supply opportunities on State contracts.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DGS is the primary operational support and procurement agency for the State, managing state-owned facilities and overseeing maintenance contracts. It is directly responsible for incorporating the expanded requirement to procure packaged or repackaged janitorial products from Blind Industries and Services of Maryland into state janitorial and maintenance contracts.

DBM assists in supervising budget execution, state procurement policies, and operational planning. As an agency providing fiscal and operational oversight, DBM was consulted on the implementation and potential impact of the bill on state procurement units.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state procurement contracts and capital and maintenance expenditures governed by the State Finance and Procurement Article, under which these preference provisions are codified.

bill_summary: Establishes the Maryland Inventory of Cemeteries and Burial Sites Workgroup to study and make recommendations on the creation, operation, and maintenance of a statewide cemetery inventory system.
responsible_party: Maryland Historical Trust
stakeholders: Cemetery operators, religious and local cemeteries, descendant communities, historical and genealogical organizations, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $42,200 in FY 2026 only to cover salary, fringe benefits, and operating expenses for one temporary contractual staff member at the Maryland Historical Trust. State revenues and local government finances are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Historical Trust (MHT), a unit of the Department of Planning, is the primary agency tasked with staffing the Workgroup. Additionally, the Director of MHT serves on the Workgroup, and the department incurs the fiscal impact associated with hiring contractual staff to support the Workgroup.

The Executive Director of the Office of Cemetery Oversight (housed within MD Labor) is a designated member of the Workgroup, and the Secretary of Labor is responsible for appointing several members representing local governments, genealogical organizations, descendant communities, and cemeteries.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill formally creates a temporary study body, the Maryland Inventory of Cemeteries and Burial Sites Workgroup, which operates through June 30, 2026, to study and issue recommendations on a state cemetery inventory system.
The Chief of the Office of Cultural Resources within the Maryland Department of Transportation (or their designee) is designated as a statutory member of the Workgroup.
The Maryland State Archivist (or their designee) is designated as a statutory member of the Workgroup.

The Office of the Attorney General is expected to handle legal research and analysis related to reviewing statutory definitions and legal requirements for the Workgroup using existing budgeted resources.
The Workgroup is required to submit its final report and policy recommendations regarding the establishment and maintenance of a cemetery inventory system to the Governor by December 1, 2025.

stakeholders: Frederick County barbershops, beauty salons holding beer and wine licenses, and their customers
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. The bill does not materially affect Frederick County finances or operations, and the impact on small businesses is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry. While the bill specifically adjusts the per-glass serving size limitation for local Frederick County barbershop and beauty salon beer and wine licenses without a state fiscal impact, it relates generally to the state's broader alcoholic beverage framework.

The Maryland Department of Labor oversees the professional licensing boards that issue barbershop and beauty salon permits under the Business Occupations and Professions Article cited in the bill, though the bill does not alter their licensing standards or operations.

bill_summary: Beginning January 1, 2027, this bill prohibits keeping an individually maintained rooster movement-constrained through the use of tethering or certain confinement enclosures. The bill establishes civil penalties for violations (ranging from warnings up to $1,000 per rooster for subsequent offenses) and provides exceptions for commercial poultry producers, schools, animal shelters, animal welfare organizations, qualifying 4-H or Future Farmers of America members, and keepers who maintain more adult hens than roosters.
responsible_party: State and local law enforcement officers and local animal control authorities
stakeholders: Rooster and poultry owners, commercial poultry producers, 4-H and Future Farmers of America members, animal welfare organizations, and local animal control and law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may experience a potential minimal increase from civil penalties, while State enforcement is expected to be handled within existing resources. Local government expenditures for local animal control and law enforcement may increase minimally in some jurisdictions; local revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary State law enforcement agency, Maryland State Police officers are expressly authorized under the bill to enforce the civil restrictions on keeping movement-constrained roosters.
The bill creates civil infractions and monetary penalties for unlawful confinement of roosters, which are processed and adjudicated through the Maryland District Court system.

Although direct regulatory and inspection mandates were removed by amendment during the legislative process, the bill directly concerns poultry management and avian flu concerns, and exempts commercial poultry operations defined under the Agriculture Article.

Synopsis: Altering certain provisions of law governing the State Board of Chiropractic Examiners and the practice of chiropractic in the State related to Board membership, licensure of chiropractors, the discipline of chiropractors, and the denial of licenses to applicants; authorizing the Board to inspect chiropractor offices under certain circumstances; and requiring the Board to require a licensee or applicant to submit to an examination by a health care provider under certain circumstances.
Title: Health Occupations - State Board of Chiropractic Examiners - Revisions

bill_summary: This bill revises the Maryland Chiropractic Act by altering the appointment process for State Board of Chiropractic Examiners members, updating licensing and examination requirements, repealing extern licenses in favor of preceptorships and temporary licenses, expanding grounds for disciplinary action, and authorizing the Board to perform unannounced office inspections for infection control guidelines and require competency evaluations for licensees or applicants suspected of causing harm.
responsible_party: State Board of Chiropractic Examiners
stakeholders: Licensed chiropractors, applicants for chiropractic licensure, chiropractic students entering preceptorships, and chiropractic patients in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: State operational requirements can be handled within existing budgeted resources. There is a potential minimal general fund revenue increase from civil penalties of up to $5,000 imposed in disciplinary proceedings. Criminal history record check fees collected by CJIS-CR will offset processing costs. Board special fund expenditures decrease minimally from the repeal of the newspaper publication requirement for examinations, while costs for required health care provider examinations are expected to be minimal and covered by existing funds. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Chiropractic Examiners is a health occupations licensing board housed within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly alters the board's composition, licensing criteria, disciplinary grounds, examination standards, and regulatory oversight.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department's Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository (CJIS-CR) processes state and national criminal history records checks, which are mandated by the bill for applicants seeking temporary chiropractic licenses.

The Governor appoints the chiropractor and consumer members of the State Board of Chiropractic Examiners. The bill modifies the appointment process, including nomination thresholds and list requirements.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in vetting, managing, and recommending appointments to state boards, including the newly altered nomination mechanisms for chiropractor members of the Board.

Synopsis: Authorizing a certain holder of a Class C beer, wine, and liquor license in Anne Arundel County to convert the license to a Class C (veterans' organization) license; reducing from $400 to $300 the annual license fee for a Class C (veterans' organization) license; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Anne Arundel County to provide application and administrative fee discounts to certain licensees and applicants; and authorizing a Class C (veterans' organization) licensee to operate on Sunday without a Sunday license.
Title: Anne Arundel County - Alcoholic Beverages Licenses - Veterans' Organizations

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: Authorizes qualifying veterans' organizations in Anne Arundel County holding a Class C beer, wine, and liquor license to convert their license to a Class C (veterans' organization) license as a renewal. The bill lowers the annual license fee from $400 to $300, permits sales on Sundays without obtaining a separate Sunday license, and authorizes the local licensing board to offer application and administrative fee discounts to qualifying veterans' organizations.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Anne Arundel County
stakeholders: Veterans' organizations and clubs in Anne Arundel County holding or applying for Class C alcoholic beverages licenses, and their members.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Anne Arundel County revenues are estimated to decrease by $2,400 annually beginning in fiscal year 2026 because an estimated eight qualifying organizations will convert to the lower-cost license ($300 vs. $480) and will no longer need to pay the $120 Sunday sales permit fee. County expenditures are not affected.

Synopsis: Requiring a custodian of recorded images produced by certain automated enforcement systems to deny inspection of the images, subject to certain exceptions; prohibiting certain State and local agencies from using a recorded image or associated data from an automated enforcement system subject to certain exceptions; and establishing certain requirements and authorizations for the removal and destruction of recorded images and associated data produced by an automated enforcement system.
Title: Motor Vehicles - Automated Enforcement Programs - Privacy Protections

bill_summary: House Bill 516 establishes privacy protections, data security standards, and retention limits for images and data captured by automated traffic enforcement systems, such as speed and red light cameras. It prohibits agencies from accessing or using recorded data without a warrant, subpoena, or court order unless used for an appropriate traffic enforcement purpose or an authorized, documented legitimate law enforcement purpose. The bill bans biometric and facial recognition technology on automated systems, mandates immediate destruction of recordings that do not show a violation, sets time limits on retaining violation records, and prohibits public inspection under Maryland's Public Information Act with limited exceptions.
responsible_party: State and local law enforcement agencies and entities operating automated enforcement programs (including the Department of State Police, the State Highway Administration, and local police departments), in consultation with the District Court of Maryland.
stakeholders: Motorists, vehicle owners, and pedestrians in Maryland whose images may be captured by traffic cameras, as well as State and local law enforcement agencies and camera system contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local governments may experience increased administrative and operational costs to establish audit procedures, train personnel, upgrade storage software to be independent and secure, and manage record destruction timelines. Agencies that knowingly violate access and use restrictions face fines up to $1,000 per violation. The Judiciary can manage any additional requests for warrants, subpoenas, or court orders using existing resources. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Highway Administration is explicitly defined as an 'agency' subject to the bill's requirements. It directly implements and operates automated enforcement programs, such as work zone speed control systems, and must adhere to new privacy standards, data destruction timelines, independent storage criteria, and internal audit procedures.

The bill directly governs State police departments that operate automated enforcement systems (such as work zone speed control) and places strict legal restrictions on how law enforcement agencies may access, retain, and use recorded images and associated data for criminal investigations.

MDOT is the parent department of the State Highway Administration and oversees statewide transportation policies and infrastructure programs, including automated traffic enforcement systems regulated by the bill.

The bill mandates that the Chief Judge of the District Court adopt procedures for citations, trial of violations, and penalty collections conforming to the new privacy standards, and the court system will handle requests for warrants, subpoenas, and court orders required to access recorded images.

Synopsis: Establishing the Workgroup on the Reorganization of the Maryland Transit Administration to study reorganizing the Maryland Transit Administration; requiring the Workgroup to report its findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly on or before December 1, 2025; and requiring the Department of Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Legislative Services, to submit to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House draft legislation to effectuate the recommendations of the Workgroup.
Title: Workgroup on the Reorganization of the Maryland Transit Administration

NarrowSubjects.Name: Bonds -see also- County & Baltimore City Bonds; State Bonds
Legislation -see also- Correct Leg; Cur Leg; Emerg Bills
Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: Establishes the Workgroup on the Reorganization of the Maryland Transit Administration to study the potential reorganization of the Maryland Department of Transportation and the Maryland Transit Administration, evaluate options for maintaining local Baltimore City transit services while separating statewide transit services, and submit findings, recommendations, and draft legislation.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation and Department of Legislative Services
stakeholders: Maryland public transit riders, Baltimore City residents and transit users, and personnel of the Maryland Transit Administration and Maryland Department of Transportation.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Transportation Trust Fund expenditures increase by an estimated $324,000 in both FY 2026 and FY 2027 ($648,000 total) for consultant services to assist with legal, budgetary, and federal regulatory analyses. State revenues and local government finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDOT is directly responsible for co-staffing the workgroup, designating the chair through the Secretary of Transportation, submitting draft legislation based on the workgroup's recommendations, and funding an estimated $324,000 annually in FY 2026 and FY 2027 for reorganization consultant studies.

MTA is the central subject of the bill, which establishes a workgroup to study reorganizing the agency's services, contractual obligations, and governance structure. The Maryland Transit Administrator serves as a member of the workgroup.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a temporary advisory body, the Workgroup on the Reorganization of the Maryland Transit Administration, to study and make recommendations regarding the restructuring of MDOT and MTA.
The Governor is tasked with appointing two members who regularly use MTA transit services to the workgroup and will receive the workgroup's final report and recommendations by December 1, 2026.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in vetting and processing candidates for gubernatorial appointments to state boards, commissions, and task forces, including the two transit user seats created by this bill.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Transit Administration to develop and implement a program providing for the first month after transit service begins on the Purple Line, free ridership on Purple Line transit vehicles to individuals residing within a one-quarter-mile radius of the Purple Line track; and requiring the Administration to include, beginning on October 1, 2025, for 3 months after service on the Purple Lines begins promotional materials and services at no cost to small businesses located within a one-quarter-mile radius of the Purple Line track.
Title: Maryland Transit Administration - Purple Line - Free Ridership and Promotional Materials and Services

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc

bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Transit Administration to develop and implement a program offering free Purple Line transit ridership for the first month of service to individuals residing within a quarter-mile of the track, and free promotional materials and services to small businesses located within a quarter-mile of the track from October 1, 2025, until three months after transit service begins.
responsible_party: Maryland Transit Administration
stakeholders: Individuals and small businesses located within a 0.25-mile radius of the Purple Line track.
fiscal_impact_summary: Transportation Trust Fund revenues decrease by an estimated $75,000 in FY 2028 due to foregone fare revenues during the initial month of operations. Transportation Trust Fund expenditures are expected to increase from FY 2026 through FY 2028 to design and provide promotional materials and services to eligible small businesses, though the exact expenditure increase cannot be predicted in advance. There is no direct impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) is directly responsible for developing, implementing, and adopting regulations for the program to provide free Purple Line ridership to qualifying residents and promotional materials and services to qualifying small businesses, which directly reduces its farebox revenue and impacts internal resources.

As the parent department of the Maryland Transit Administration, the Maryland Department of Transportation oversees transit operations and manages the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF), which will experience a decrease in revenues and an increase in operational expenditures as a result of this bill.

Synopsis: Prohibiting, from October 1, 2025, to July 1, 2028, a person from driving a motor vehicle in violation of certain provisions of the Maryland Vehicle Law on private roadways in a certain residential community in Baltimore County; authorizing, from October 1, 2025, to July 1, 2028, a police officer to enforce the vehicle law on private roadways in a certain residential community in Baltimore County; and prohibiting a person from driving a motor vehicle in violation of the Act on any roadway located in certain areas of Calvert County.
Title: Baltimore County - Vehicle Laws - Private Roadways in Residential Communities

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: Authorizes police officers in Baltimore County, from October 1, 2025, to July 1, 2028, to enforce Maryland Vehicle Law on private roadways in the Queen Anne Village community in Owings Mills, prohibiting vehicle law violations on those roads during that period. It also requires the Baltimore County Police Department to report on the bill's implementation and impact by September 1, 2028.
responsible_party: Baltimore County Police Department
stakeholders: Drivers, residents, and visitors in the Queen Anne Village community in Owings Mills, as well as Baltimore County law enforcement officers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances and operations are not materially affected. Baltimore County can likely handle enforcement within existing resources, and local revenues are not affected. Although the Baltimore County Police Department advised that hiring additional officers would be needed, the Department of Legislative Services noted that the enforcement authority is discretionary and limited in scope, meaning existing resources should suffice.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Maryland Transportation Article regarding the application and enforcement of the Maryland Vehicle Law on private roadways in specific communities.

As a statewide law enforcement agency responsible for enforcing motor vehicle laws, the Maryland State Police is technically authorized under the broad statutory definition of police officers to enforce vehicle laws in the designated private roadway area, though primary enforcement is expected to be handled locally by Baltimore County.

Synopsis: Authorizing a judge to consider whether a military protection order has been issued against a respondent when determining whether to grant a temporary peace order or a temporary protective order; and requiring a law enforcement officer to notify a certain law enforcement agency that an individual may have violated a military protection order under certain circumstances.
Title: Peace Orders and Protective Orders – Military Protection Orders

NarrowSubjects.Name: Armed Forces -see also- Military Department; Veterans
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: Authorizes judges to consider whether a military protection order (MPO) has been issued against a respondent when deciding whether to grant a temporary peace order or temporary protective order. Additionally requires law enforcement officers to notify the entering agency if they have probable cause to believe a service member has violated both a state peace or protective order and an MPO listed in the FBI's National Crime Information Center database.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts) and Maryland law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Petitioners and victims seeking protective or peace orders, military service members subject to military protection orders, and state and local law enforcement officers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Judiciary increase by $99,900 in FY 2026 only for one-time computer programming costs. State revenues are not affected. The bill is not anticipated to materially impact local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the judicial branch by authorizing District and Circuit Court judges to consider military protection orders when determining whether to issue temporary peace or protective orders. The Administrative Office of the Courts requires $99,900 in FY 2026 for one-time computer programming and case management software modifications.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, Maryland State Police troopers are subject to the bill's mandate requiring law enforcement officers to notify the agency that entered an MPO into the FBI's NCIC database if a service member violates a peace or protective order and is suspected of violating an MPO.

The Adjutant General heads the Maryland Military Department, which was consulted as an information source for the legislation. The bill establishes statutory recognition of military protection orders issued by commanding officers within the military forces.
The Maryland National Guard is explicitly referenced in the statutory definition of a 'military protection order' issued by commanding officers against personnel under their command.

Synopsis: Establishing the Abandoned and Neglected Cemeteries Fund to provide for the care, preservation, maintenance, and restoration of abandoned and neglected cemeteries in the State; authorizing the Governor to include in the annual budget bill an appropriation of $250,000 to the fund; and requiring an annual report by September 30 to the General Assembly on the donations to the Fund and promotional efforts undertaken by money from the Fund.
Title: Abandoned and Neglected Cemeteries Fund - Establishment

bill_summary: Establishes the Abandoned and Neglected Cemeteries Fund to support the care, preservation, maintenance, and restoration of abandoned and neglected cemeteries across Maryland. Administered by the Secretary of Labor, the fund may receive an optional annual state budget appropriation of up to $250,000, as well as interest earnings and other donations.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Communities with neglected or abandoned burial grounds, descendants and families of those interred in neglected cemeteries, and cemetery preservation organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: General fund expenditures increase by $250,000 annually beginning in FY 2026 if the Governor exercises the discretion to appropriate that amount to the fund. Special fund revenues and expenditures for the Maryland Department of Labor increase correspondingly by $250,000 annually to carry out the fund's purposes and administration. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Labor is designated to administer the newly established Abandoned and Neglected Cemeteries Fund, oversee expenditures for cemetery maintenance and restoration, and submit an annual report to the General Assembly.
The State Treasurer is statutorily required to hold the Abandoned and Neglected Cemeteries Fund separately and invest its moneys in the same manner as other State funds.
The Comptroller is required to account for the Abandoned and Neglected Cemeteries Fund and its interest earnings.
The bill explicitly authorizes the Governor to include a discretionary appropriation of $250,000 to the Fund in the annual budget bill.

Synopsis: Requiring the Family Investment Administration in the Department of Human Services to be the central coordinating and directing agency of the federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program using certain funds and resources; and repealing the requirement that the Secretary of Aging administer the Program.
Title: Department of Human Services - Federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program - Administration

NarrowSubjects.Name: Public Benefits -see also- FoodStmps; Housing; MedAsst

bill_summary: This bill transfers the administration and coordination of the federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program from the Maryland Department of Aging to the Family Investment Administration within the Department of Human Services.
responsible_party: Family Investment Administration in the Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Low-income seniors aged 60 and older receiving supplemental food packages, the Department of Human Services, the Maryland Department of Aging, and partner food distribution organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: Overall federal fund revenues and expenditures are unaffected but are transferred from the Maryland Department of Aging (MDOA) to the Department of Human Services (DHS), shifting approximately $225,000 in FY 2026 and $300,000 annually thereafter. MDOA general fund expenditures increase by approximately $22,000 in FY 2026 and $29,000 annually thereafter to cover salary costs for a program coordinator previously funded by federal funds. Local finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Family Investment Administration within the Department of Human Services as the central coordinating and directing agency for the federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program, transferring program administration and approximately $300,000 in annual federal funding to the department.

The bill repeals the requirement that the Secretary of Aging administer the Commodity Supplemental Food Program, resulting in a reduction in federal funding previously used for administrative costs and necessitating an increase in general fund expenditures to support existing staff.

Synopsis: Establishing a nonprofit organizations navigator within the Department of Commerce to provide technical assistance and work with nonprofits and units of State government to resolve complexities and delays in State grant-making processes, collect and share certain information, and represent nonprofit organizations' interests and concerns as a member of the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council; and requiring the Department to report to certain committees of the General Assembly on the implementation of the navigator.
Title: Department of Commerce - Nonprofit Organizations Navigator - Established

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

NarrowSubjects.Name: Communications -see also- ElecComm; Intergov; Telecom; etc.

Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: Establishes a Nonprofit Organizations Navigator within the Department of Commerce to provide technical assistance to nonprofits applying for state grant programs, assist in resolving grant-making delays, share grant opportunity information, and serve on the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council.
responsible_party: Department of Commerce
stakeholders: Nonprofit organizations in Maryland seeking or managing state, federal, and local grants
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $80,400 in FY 2026 and $69,800 in FY 2027 to fund one contractual navigator position in the Department of Commerce. The FY 2026 budget includes $80,400 for this position. State revenues are unaffected, and there is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 541 directly establishes the Nonprofit Organizations Navigator within the Department of Commerce, requiring the Secretary to designate the position, manage its operations, and submit a detailed performance report by January 1, 2027. It also creates a direct fiscal impact on the department for staffing and operating costs.

DBM chairs and staffs the Maryland Efficient Grant Application (MEGA) Council, which receives the navigator as a nonvoting member. Additionally, the bill alters MEGA Council duties and repeals prior statutory reporting requirements that required DBM to report to the General Assembly regarding a State Grants Ombudsperson.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the membership and statutory duties of an executive council—the Maryland Efficient Grant Application (MEGA) Council—by adding the navigator to its membership and repealing the requirement for the council to study and report on a State Grants Ombudsperson.

Synopsis: Authorizing a local department of social services to request assistance from federal law enforcement officers in an investigation relating to an alleged vulnerable adult; and altering certain provisions relating to the disclosure of certain information concerning human services to include adult protective services.
Title: Adult Protective Services - Investigations and Disclosure of Information

bill_summary: Authorizes local departments of social services to request assistance from federal law enforcement officers when conducting investigations concerning alleged vulnerable adults, and extends statutory confidentiality and disclosure protections to adult protective services records and information.
responsible_party: Department of Human Services (including local departments of social services)
stakeholders: Alleged vulnerable adults, recipients and applicants of adult protective services, local departments of social services, and federal law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local entities participating in investigations regarding vulnerable adults may experience operational efficiencies; however, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHS oversees the State's local departments of social services, which administer the Adult Protective Services (APS) program. The bill directly impacts DHS by authorizing local departments to request assistance from federal law enforcement during vulnerable adult investigations and amending confidentiality and disclosure laws concerning APS records.

The Department of Aging works closely with adult protective services and is statutorily authorized to assist local departments in vulnerable adult investigations, and it serves as an advisory body on adult protective policies.

Synopsis: Establishing a certain appeal process for persons who are subject to the digital advertising gross revenues tax and receive a notice of assessment from the Comptroller; authorizing the Comptroller or the Comptroller's designee to issue an order to correct an erroneous assessment of the digital advertising gross revenues tax, subject to certain conditions; and applying the Act to assessments of the digital advertising gross revenues tax made after December 31, 2025.
Title: Digital Advertising Gross Revenues Tax - Assessments - Appeals and Corrections

NarrowSubjects.Name: Electronic Commerce -see also- Electronic Funds Transfer

bill_summary: Establishes an administrative appeal and correction process for taxpayers subject to the digital advertising gross revenues tax who receive an assessment from the Comptroller, authorizing informal hearings and enabling the Comptroller to correct or abate erroneous assessments in the same manner as other state taxes.
responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Businesses subject to Maryland's digital advertising gross revenues tax that receive tax assessments, tax attorneys, and the Comptroller's Office.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $132,100 in FY 2026 (reflecting hiring two senior tax attorneys with a 180-day start-up delay), growing to $229,400 in FY 2027 and $260,900 by FY 2030 for ongoing operating expenses and salaries. State revenues are not directly affected. There is no local government fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Comptroller's Office with administering an informal appeals process, holding hearings, issuing notices of final determination, and correcting erroneous assessments for the digital advertising gross revenues tax. The Comptroller requires additional personnel and expenditures ($132,100 in FY 2026) to manage these appeals.

The Maryland Tax Court hears appeals from final determinations of the Comptroller. Establishing a formal administrative revision, informal hearing, and assessment abatement process with the Comptroller directly affects the procedural pipeline of digital advertising gross revenues tax disputes.

Synopsis: Requiring, beginning on January 1, 2026, the Maryland Medical Assistance Program to provide coverage for self-measured blood pressure monitoring for certain eligible Program recipients; and requiring reimbursement of health care provider and other staff time used for patient training, transmission of blood pressure data, interpretation of blood pressure readings and reporting, remote patient monitoring, and the delivery of co-interventions, including educational materials or classes.
Title: Maryland Medical Assistance Program - Maternal Health Self-Measured Blood Pressure Monitoring

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs
Medical Conditions -see also- AIDS; COVID-19; rabies

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), beginning January 1, 2026, to provide coverage for self-measured blood pressure monitoring to recipients who are pregnant, postpartum, or diagnosed with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, heart disease, or a cardiometabolic disease. The required coverage includes validated home blood pressure monitors as well as reimbursement for healthcare provider and staff time for training, data transmission, interpretation, and remote monitoring.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Medicaid recipients who are pregnant, postpartum, or diagnosed with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, heart disease, or cardiometabolic disease, as well as healthcare providers and local health departments.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no meaningful State fiscal impact or material effect on revenues because Medicaid already covers self-measured blood pressure monitoring based on medical necessity regardless of diagnosis. Local health departments may receive reimbursement for healthcare provider services, with no effect on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is administered by the Maryland Department of Health, to provide coverage for self-measured blood pressure monitoring to eligible pregnant, postpartum, and chronically ill recipients, as well as submit an annual report on outcomes and costs.

Synopsis: Authorizing food establishments that are businesses that conduct agritourism, Class 4 limited wineries, or Class 8 farm breweries to comply with the requirement to provide a convenient lavatory by providing a portable chemical toilet that is supplied with approved hand drying devices, kept in a sanitary condition, is properly ventilated, and is placed at least 25 feet from a well.
Title: Food Establishments - Portable Chemical Toilets
bill_summary: Authorizes certain food establishments—specifically agritourism businesses, Class 4 limited wineries, and Class 8 farm breweries—to fulfill the requirement of providing a convenient lavatory by providing a portable chemical toilet that is ventilated, kept in a sanitary condition, equipped with hand-drying devices and soap and water, and situated at least 25 feet away from a well.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Agritourism businesses, Class 4 limited wineries, Class 8 farm breweries, and their patrons
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local revenues and expenditures are not affected. The Maryland Department of Health can update relevant regulations and issue guidance using existing budgeted resources. Local health departments can conduct necessary inspections and respond to complaints using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary regulatory agency responsible for food establishment sanitation standards under the Health - General Article. MDH must update relevant regulations (COMAR 10.15.03) and issue guidance to local health departments regarding portable chemical toilet compliance.

The Maryland Department of the Environment oversees state regulations governing chemical toilets (COMAR 26.04.02) and wellhead protection standards, which intersect directly with the bill's requirement that portable chemical toilets be placed at least 25 feet from a well.

The bill directly affects agricultural entities, including agritourism operations, Class 4 limited wineries, and Class 8 farm breweries, which fall under the Department of Agriculture's broader purview to support the economic viability of farms and agribusinesses in Maryland.

Synopsis: Altering from four to three the number of members elected from each councilmanic district of Baltimore County to the Baltimore County Republican Party Central Committee; and altering the number of members elected from each legislative district of Baltimore County to the Baltimore County Democratic Party Central Committee.
Title: Baltimore County - Political Party Central Committee - Elections
bill_summary: This bill reduces the number of members elected to the Baltimore County Republican Party Central Committee from four to three per councilmanic district and restructures the membership allocation of the Baltimore County Democratic Party Central Committee based on legislative districts wholly located in the county.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Voters and candidates for the Baltimore County Republican Party Central Committee and the Baltimore County Democratic Party Central Committee.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect State or Baltimore County finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections (SBE) is responsible for administering and supervising all elections across Maryland, including primary election ballots where political party central committee members are elected according to statutory district allocations.

Synopsis: Establishing in Dorchester County a venue beer, wine, and liquor license that authorizes the holder to sell or serve beer, wine, and liquor for on-premises consumption during an event where food is served; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Dorchester County to issue the license to certain nonprofit or for-profit retail businesses that meet certain criteria; and authorizing the issuance of a license to an establishment that is within 300 feet of a place of worship or a school with certain written consent.
Title: Dorchester County - Alcoholic Beverages - Venue Beer, Wine, and Liquor License

Food -see also- Meat, Poultry, & Seafood; Milk; etc.
Primary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Schools
Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch

bill_summary: Establishes an annual venue beer, wine, and liquor license in Dorchester County for nonprofit or for-profit retail businesses that host events such as weddings, banquets, and meetings at venues meeting certain size and capacity requirements, permitting them to sell or serve alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption when food is provided.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Dorchester County
stakeholders: Dorchester County event venue owners and operators (nonprofit and for-profit businesses), event attendees, and nearby schools and places of worship.
fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Dorchester County revenues increase beginning in FY 2026 to the extent venue beer, wine, and liquor licenses are issued at an annual fee of $1,500 each. Additional enforcement activity can be absorbed using existing county resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new retail alcoholic beverage license in Dorchester County administered by the local board of license commissioners. While the bill has no direct state fiscal effect, the Comptroller oversees statewide alcohol regulation and tax collection on alcoholic beverages.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Board of Pharmacy to send renewal notices to licensees, permit holders, and registrants by electronic means, rather than by first-class mail, unless the licensee, permit holder, or registrant requests to receive the renewal notice by first-class mail.
Title: State Board of Pharmacy - Renewal Notices - Electronic Means

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits

bill_summary: Requires the State Board of Pharmacy to send renewal notices to pharmacists, pharmacy permit holders, registered pharmacy technicians, wholesale distributor permit holders, and registered pharmacy interns by electronic means rather than first-class mail, unless first-class mail is specifically requested.
responsible_party: State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Licensed pharmacists, pharmacy permit holders, registered pharmacy technicians, wholesale distributor permit holders, and registered pharmacy interns in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Board of Pharmacy special fund expenditures decrease by an estimated $14,500 annually beginning in FY 2026 due to savings on printing and postage. State revenues and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Pharmacy is an occupational licensing and regulatory board housed within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly alters the board's renewal notice procedures to electronic delivery, reducing special fund operating expenditures for mailing and printing.

Synopsis: Altering licensing fees for certain alcoholic beverages licenses in Dorchester County; and authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Dorchester County to charge an application or transfer fee under certain circumstances.
Title: Dorchester County - Alcoholic Beverages Licenses - Fees

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: Alters annual and per diem alcoholic beverages license fees in Dorchester County, decreasing the fee for Class C beer licenses while increasing fees for several other license categories. Additionally, authorizes the Dorchester County Board of License Commissioners to charge nonrefundable application fees for new licenses ($150 or $200 depending on license type) and a $50 transfer fee.
responsible_party: Dorchester County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders, applicants, restaurants, bars, caterers, and small businesses in Dorchester County
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Dorchester County revenues will increase by at least $10,250 annually beginning in FY 2026 due to increased license fees across at least 66 existing businesses, plus additional indeterminate revenues from new application and transfer fees. County expenditures are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates aspects of the state's alcohol industry; however, this bill strictly alters local license, application, and transfer fees administered by the Board of License Commissioners for Dorchester County, having no direct state fiscal or operational impact.

bill_summary: The Educational Equality for Service Members Act establishes uniform definitions for military-related terms across the Maryland Code (Education, General Provisions, and State Government Articles), aligning them primarily with federal definitions in the U.S. Code. It broadens various education-related benefits and privileges—previously limited largely to the armed forces—to encompass all uniformed services (including the Public Health Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration commissioned corps), their active duty members, veterans, and their eligible dependents. These benefits include public school enrollment exceptions, expedited teacher licensing, emergency medical services credentialing credits, in-state tuition exemptions, and state scholarship eligibility.

stakeholders: Active-duty and reserve members of the uniformed services (including the armed forces, Public Health Service, and NOAA), veterans, their spouses, and dependent children.
